segments.source: Terrain energy costs per segment: {'plain': 1, 'forest': 2, 'hill': 3, 'marsh': 4}. Three routes from Elm to Stone: R1=['plain', 'hill', 'plain']; R2=['forest', 'forest', 'plain']; R3=['plain', 'marsh']. The traveler can spend at most 10 energy units.
The energy of a route is the sum of its terrain costs. A route above the energy limit is infeasible. Among feasible routes, minimize energy.
Which route is feasible and uses the least energy?
1. Compute route totals: R1=5, R2=5, R3=5. 2. Discard any total above 10. 3. The smallest remaining total is R1=5.
Relief changes the cost of movement; “shortest” and “easiest” are not automatically the same.
Weighted paths with a feasibility budget; sum costs and choose the minimum feasible path.

Problem 536. Classifying climate data: Station A
Climate descriptions summarize long-term patterns. In a reasoning problem, explicit thresholds let us classify numerical data without hidden knowledge.

Use this classroom classification: cool if mean temperature <12°C; mild if 12–17°C; warm if >17°C. Dry if annual precipitation <500 mm; wet if ≥500 mm. Data: Station A: T=8°C, P=490 mm; Station B: T=16°C, P=760 mm; Station C: T=12°C, P=520 mm.
Apply only the stated thresholds. Temperature and precipitation are separate dimensions, so each station receives two labels.
Classify Station A. Then identify whether any other station has the same two-label class.
1. Compare T=8 with the temperature thresholds: it is cool. 2. Compare P=490 with 500 mm: it is dry. 3. Compare the combined label with the other stations; matches: none.
Station A is cool and dry; no other station has the same class.
Classification is the application of clear predicates to data; the rule must be stated before the label is inferred.
Numeric predicates with thresholds; output the conjunction of the temperature and precipitation categories.

Problem 541. Bottlenecks in the Iris–Pine exchange network
Trade and transport networks have capacities. A single narrow connection can limit a much larger network.
Goods move from Iris to Pine along two branches: Iris→Kite capacity 6, Kite→Pine capacity 5; Iris→Birch capacity 2, Birch→Pine capacity 7. The final warehouse at Pine can accept at most 9 units.
A branch cannot carry more than its smallest edge capacity. Independent branch capacities can be added, but a shared destination capacity can cap the total.
What is the maximum number of units that can reach Pine in one period? Identify the bottleneck(s).
1. Branch 1 is limited by min(6,5)=5. 2. Branch 2 is limited by min(2,7)=2. 3. Together the branches could carry 7 units. 4. The destination accepts at most 9, so the final maximum is min(7,9)=7.
A bottleneck is a local limit that constrains the total possible flow.
Flow network; branch capacity is a minimum along a path; total is the sum of independent branches subject to shared caps.
